A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RFWave and retain identifiable corresponding architecture, equations, and experiments. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original waveform-reconstruction scores, domain and loss ablations, spectrogram comparisons, and inference-speed measurements in Tables 1–3 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 reports original Mel-spectrogram and EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, human listening evaluations, ablations, and efficiency measurements, including detailed appendix results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces overlapping subbands with a consistency loss, an STFT loss applied to the estimated clean signal, and classifier-free guidance, including its use for EnCodec reconstruction. These change training and inference. The shared ConvNeXtV2 backbone remains, and v1's time-balanced loss is renamed energy-balanced with the same Equation 5. EnCodec conditioning was already described in v1.

E1.justification: v2 retains the principal Mel-reconstruction datasets but removes the Universal-dataset experiment. It adds actual EnCodec-token reconstruction experiments, training with Common Voice, DNS Challenge speech, Jamendo, FSD50K, and AudioSet. The external evaluation suite in Table A.4 substantially broadens coverage across speech, vocals, and sound effects.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares RFWave with Vocos. v2 adds evaluated PriorGrad and FreGrad comparisons for Mel reconstruction and EnCodec and Multi-Band Diffusion comparisons for token reconstruction. Vocos also becomes a comparator in the Jamendo experiment, where v1 reports only RFWave. The speed comparison expands accordingly.

E3.justification: v2 replaces UTMOS and Mel-SNR evaluation with human MOS, ViSQOL, voiced/unvoiced F1, and periodicity error, while retaining PESQ. Jamendo testing changes from 1,397 files to 50. New codec experiments evaluate bandwidths from 1.5 to 12 kbps. CPU timing is removed, while the RTX 4090, batch-one LJSpeech GPU benchmark is retained.

E4.justification: The retained time/frequency-domain and balanced-loss ablation is expanded with overlap-loss, STFT-loss, and guidance combinations in v2 Table 3. Appendix A.3 expands spectrogram case studies to additional methods and music artifacts. Conversely, v1's 100-step sampling comparison and 80-versus-100-dimensional Mel-input comparison disappear.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 adds uncertainty to human MOS results, explicitly identifying 95% confidence intervals in Table 1 and displaying intervals in the detailed results. This is a new reporting practice, but training-seed replication, listener counts, and interval-construction procedures are not specified.

E6.justification: v2 substantially replaces and expands the reported results, adding MOS, codec-bandwidth results, and new ablation outcomes. For example, Table 1 reports average MOS of 3.95 for RFWave, 3.47 for Vocos, and 3.75 for PriorGrad. Reported RFWave GPU throughput changes from 91.46 to 97.01 times real-time. Universal, CPU, and preliminary direct-TTS results disappear. Many quality scores use revised configurations or test subsets and therefore do not establish controlled performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: The original Rectified Flow formulation and balanced-loss Equation 5 remain. v2 adds formal overlap/subband dimension definitions and Equations 6–7 connecting predicted velocity to an estimated clean signal for STFT-loss computation. These are limited mathematical additions; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 broadens the abstract's reconstruction claim from Mel-spectrograms to Mel-spectrograms or discrete tokens. The contributions now emphasize three enhanced losses and reduced GPU memory use, and the introduction newly claims the fastest diffusion-based waveform reconstruction to the authors' knowledge. The headline speed changes from approximately 90 to 97 times real-time.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for stronger guidance effects with tokens, the STFT loss's magnitude-versus-phase tradeoff, and ViSQOL's apparent preference for GAN outputs despite audible artifacts. It also discusses bandwidth saturation and MBD's sound-effect performance. v1's disclosure that preliminary direct text-to-complex-spectrogram TTS underperformed a cascade is removed, although the proposed future direction remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds auxiliary-loss weights and their gradient-norm rationale, overlap size, codec feature-extraction settings, training hardware and durations, baseline repository links, and detailed external-test construction instructions. Existing optimizer, crop, batch-size, and backbone details largely move to Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's direct RFWave repository link and explicit TTS-checkpoint availability statement are omitted; this does not establish that the resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around neural codecs and diffusion competitors through discussions of PriorGrad, FreGrad, SoundStream, VALL-E, and UniAudio, and adds flow-matching TTS context. The earlier Parallel WaveNet, ClariNet, and WaveGrad discussion disappears. Together with the new fastest-diffusion claim, this changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic maintenance.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, the method is reorganized into model structure and loss functions, and the results place application comparisons before ablations. Implementation details move into a structured appendix with separate resources, examples, and tables sections. Terminology and the author block also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overlap schematic, restructures results into aggregate and detailed tables, and expands the compact spectrogram comparison into three appendix figures with ground truth and additional methods. The weighting plot is redrawn, the model schematic is restyled, and resource and dataset-construction tables are added. Page geometry and headers also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v1's central quality and efficiency claims relied largely on automatic metrics and comparison with Vocos. v2 adds human listening evidence with uncertainty, direct diffusion competitors, codec reconstruction tests, and ablations addressing the new losses and guidance. These substantially strengthen support for the paper's central claims, while the appendix improves reproducibility. Listener counts and confidence-interval procedures remain unspecified, and removal of the negative preliminary TTS result and direct code/checkpoint disclosures weakens transparency. Those losses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
